title: Easy read and accessible information
blurb: Write and use easy read information, reinforce it through repetition and praise, and meet the Accessible Information Standard.
question: Shona, 26, has a mild learning disability and is starting a new inhaler. The ward's patient leaflet is four pages of small print. What makes information accessible to her, and what must the nurse record?

teach.body: Easy read was created to help people with learning disabilities understand information. It uses clear images to support the meaning of simple, jargon-free text and focuses on the most important information. It differs from plain English: it is shorter, explains any hard word, and pairs each point with a picture. In plain English: one idea, simple words, a picture that shows it.
teach.cite: Cabinet Office Disability Unit, Accessible communication formats (GOV.UK, updated June 2026)

teach.caption: GOV.UK example: 'We need to see the poster before we put it up... Offend means to upset people.'

head: Do
Avoid
rows: Test it with the people it is for
teach.caption: Easy read should be developed with its audience. Organisations often commission it from expert groups.

teach.body: Under the Equality Act 2010, the reasonable adjustments a provider must make include steps to provide information in an accessible format (s20(6)), and the disabled person must not be charged for them (s20(7)). NICE NG11 asks for information in spoken and picture formats and written Easy Read versions, using different colours and fonts as needed. The Accessible Information Standard (updated 2025) applies to NHS and publicly funded adult social care, including carers and parents.
teach.cite: Equality Act 2010 s20(5)-(7); NICE NG11 1.1.1; AIS DAPB1605

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: The need, not just the diagnosis

teach.body: Accessible information is rarely understood in one go. Give it in small chunks, go through the easy read together, repeat key points on different days and in different ways, and check with teach-back. Praise each step the person gets right: positive reinforcement builds confidence and memory. Leave the easy read with the person and share it with their carers, who can talk it through again later (NMC Annexe A 2.6).
teach.cite: NMC Annexe A 2.6; GOV.UK easy read guidance

teach.h: Scenario: Shona and her new inhaler
teach.body: Shona, 26, is starting a new inhaler. The nurse records that she needs easy read and extra time, and flags it. She uses an easy read sheet with one step per picture: 'Shake the inhaler', 'Breathe out', and so on. She shows each step, Shona copies it, and the nurse praises each correct step. They repeat it the next morning. Shona takes the sheet home, and with her consent a copy goes to her GP and support worker.

teach.text: Easy read is not 'plain English with clip art', and handing over a leaflet is not the same as making information accessible. The need must also be recorded, flagged and shared, or the next service starts again from nothing that helps.

items: Easy read: simple jargon-free text, one idea per sentence, clear images beside the text.
Explain hard words; keep to the most important information; test with the audience.
Accessible formats are a reasonable adjustment, free of charge (Equality Act s20).
AIS: identify, record, flag, share, meet, review.
Repeat, practise and praise: understanding builds over time.

summary: You can now tell easy read from plain English, write and use easy read information well, and reinforce learning with repetition and praise. You can meet the Accessible Information Standard by recording, flagging and sharing the person's communication needs.

A.q: A nurse is adapting a discharge leaflet into easy read for a man with a learning disability. Which feature is most characteristic of easy read?
options: Short simple sentences with a clear image beside each point
A larger font size with the full original text unchanged
Plain English paragraphs with headings and bullet points
A summary in medical terms with a glossary at the end
A.why: Easy read uses clear images to support the meaning of simple, jargon-free text, focused on the most important information.

whyNot.1: Large print helps people with sight loss but does not simplify the content.
whyNot.2: Plain English is clearer than standard text but is not easy read.
whyNot.3: Medical terms with a glossary keep the jargon in the main text.

A.q: Which list shows the steps of the Accessible Information Standard in order?
options: Assess, plan, implement, evaluate, review, close
Identify, record, flag, share, meet, review
Ask, inform, consent, record, share, review
Identify, refer, assess, flag, treat, review
A.why: The Standard (updated 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs, and to review them.

whyNot.0: That is a nursing process cycle, not the AIS steps.
whyNot.2: Consent is not one of the AIS steps.
whyNot.3: Referral and treatment are not AIS steps.

A.q: A clinic manager asks whether the person can be charged for producing an easy read version of a letter. What does the Equality Act 2010 say?
options: A charge is allowed if the cost is reasonable
The charge falls to the person's local authority
The person must not be charged for the adjustment
A charge is allowed for any second or later copy
A.why: Section 20(7) of the Equality Act 2010 says a disabled person must not be required to pay for a reasonable adjustment, including accessible information.

whyNot.0: No charge may be passed to the disabled person, however reasonable.
whyNot.1: The service provider bears the cost, not the person's local authority.
whyNot.3: The no-charge rule applies to the adjustment, not just the first copy.

B.q: A nurse writes an easy read sentence: 'The doctor will do a colonoscopy.' Which revision best fits easy read guidance?
options: The doctor will do a colonoscopy (endoscopic examination).
A colonoscopy is an investigation of the lower bowel.
The doctor will do a test called a colonoscopy, see glossary.
The doctor will look inside your bottom with a camera.
B.why: Easy read uses everyday words and explains what will happen, with a picture beside it. The hard word can be added and explained once if the person will hear it used.

whyNot.0: Adding another technical term in brackets makes it harder.
whyNot.2: Sending the reader to a glossary breaks the flow; explain the word where it appears.

B.q: Kemal, 34, has a mild learning disability and is learning to check his blood glucose. He gets the first three steps right. What is the best way to reinforce his learning?
options: Praise the steps he has done well and repeat later
Wait to praise him until he completes the whole task
Correct the remaining steps by doing them for him
Give him the manufacturer's booklet to read tonight
B.why: Positive reinforcement of each correct step, with repetition over time, builds confidence and memory (Annexe A 2.6).

whyNot.1: Holding praise back until the end misses the chance to reinforce progress.
whyNot.2: Doing it for him removes the practice he needs.
whyNot.3: A standard manufacturer booklet is unlikely to be accessible to him.

B.q: A GP practice records 'learning disability' on a patient's notes but nothing else. Which AIS requirement is not being met?
options: Identifying that the person has a disability
Recording the specific communication need
Reviewing the diagnosis every year
Sharing the diagnosis with the local council
B.why: The Standard requires the information and communication need itself (for example 'needs easy read and appointments explained by phone') to be recorded, not just the diagnosis.

whyNot.0: The disability has been identified; the specific need has not been recorded.
whyNot.2: The review step concerns communication needs, not re-checking a diagnosis.
whyNot.3: Sharing is with services involved in care, and it is the need that is shared.

C.q: Shona, 26, has a mild learning disability. She has an easy read sheet for her new inhaler and shows the nurse each step correctly on the ward. She is being discharged tomorrow. Which action best completes the nurse's duties?
options: Discharge her with the standard manufacturer's leaflet
Ask her to return to the ward to repeat the teaching
Give the easy read to her and share her needs onward
Arrange for a district nurse to give her inhaler daily
C.why: Shona keeps the easy read for repetition at home, and her recorded communication needs are shared (with consent) with her GP and support worker so they are met there too.

whyNot.0: The standard leaflet is not accessible to her.
whyNot.1: She has shown she can do it; returning to the ward is unnecessary.
whyNot.3: She is able to use the inhaler; taking over the task removes her independence.

C.q: A trust produces an easy read leaflet about bowel screening. Feedback shows people with a learning disability still find it confusing. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add the full clinical detail from the adult leaflet
Translate the leaflet into several community languages
Increase the font size and use a yellow background
Revise it with people with a learning disability
C.why: GOV.UK guidance says easy read should be developed in consultation with its audience. Testing and revising with people with a learning disability is the way to make it work.

whyNot.0: Easy read focuses on the most important information; full clinical detail adds confusion.
whyNot.1: Language translation does not solve a learning disability access problem.
whyNot.2: Format changes may help some readers but do not fix confusing content.

C.q: Mo, 40, has a moderate learning disability and lives with his father, who has sight loss. A hospital letter about Mo's appointment arrives in standard print. Under the AIS, whose needs should the hospital record?
options: Mo's needs, and his father's as his carer
Mo's needs, as the patient named on the letter
His father's needs, as the person reading the letter
Neither, as a phone call can replace the letter
C.why: The Accessible Information Standard covers patients and their carers and parents, so both Mo's and his father's information needs should be identified, recorded and met.

whyNot.1: The Standard also covers carers whose own needs affect access to information.
whyNot.2: Mo's own needs must be met; the letter is about his care.
whyNot.3: A call may be part of meeting the need, but the needs still have to be recorded.

reteach.title: One idea, one picture
reteach.question: If you had to explain a hospital test to someone using as few words as possible, what would you keep and what would you cut?

blocks.body: Keep what the person needs to know and do. Cut background, jargon and detail they do not need now. Put each idea in its own short sentence with a picture that shows it. If you must use a hard word, explain it straight away.

rows.label: Text
values: Please fast from midnight prior to your procedure
Do not eat after 12 at night

blocks.text: Producing the leaflet is only half the job: record, flag and share the need so the next appointment letter arrives in easy read too.

explain.body: Clear images support simple, jargon-free text focused on the most important information. Different from plain English.

test.q: How does easy read differ from plain English?
options: Easy read uses a larger font size throughout
Easy read uses clear images to support text
Easy read is written mainly for children
Easy read avoids any use of numbers or dates
test.why: Easy read pairs simple text with clear images and keeps to the most important information.

whyNot.0: Font size alone is large print, not easy read.
whyNot.2: Easy read is for adults and children with learning disabilities.
whyNot.3: Numbers can be used when they are needed, written simply.

explain.body: Extra support such as an easy read letter is an auxiliary aid under the third requirement of the Equality Act 2010 (s20(5)); s20(6) confirms the duty includes providing information in an accessible format, and the person cannot be charged for it (s20(7)).

test.q: Under the Equality Act 2010, an easy read appointment letter is best described as which kind of adjustment?
options: Changing a physical feature
A positive action measure under s158
Providing an auxiliary aid
Making a best interests decision
test.why: An easy read letter is extra support so a disabled person can use the service, which is the auxiliary aid requirement in s20(5); s20(6) confirms the duty includes providing information in an accessible format.

whyNot.0: Physical features are things like ramps and signage.
whyNot.1: Positive action (s158) covers voluntary steps to meet the needs of a disadvantaged group; an accessible letter is a reasonable adjustment owed under s20.
whyNot.3: Best interests decisions belong to the Mental Capacity Act.

explain.body: Identify, record, flag, share, meet and review information and communication needs. Covers patients, carers and parents.

test.q: Which AIS step makes sure a person's need is visible whenever their record is opened?
options: Identify
Review
Meet
Flag
test.why: Flagging highlights the recorded need on the record so staff see it at every contact.

whyNot.1: Reviewing checks the need is still current.

explain.body: Small chunks, practice, praise for each correct step and repetition over days help people learn and remember.

test.q: Which approach best uses positive reinforcement when teaching a new skill?
options: Praise each step the person gets right
Point out each mistake as it happens
Offer a reward at the end of the week
Show the whole task once and leave it
test.why: Praising each correct step immediately reinforces it and builds confidence.

whyNot.1: Focusing on errors is not positive reinforcement.
whyNot.2: A delayed reward is weakly linked to the behaviour.
whyNot.3: One demonstration without practice or praise rarely sticks.
